question: Why does the error middleware send a generic JSON body instead of the dependency's own error message?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki dependency ka error text hamara nahi hai, aur usme aisi cheezein ho sakti hain jo client ko kabhi nahi dikhni chahiye -- internal hostnames, IPs, tokens, stack traces. Isliye adapter sirf teen fixed bodies bhejta hai: open breaker par `{"error":"dependency_unavailable", ...}`, full bulkhead par `{"error":"overloaded", ...}`, aur timeout par `{"error":"dependency_timeout", ...}`.

Socho SMS provider ka 500 response kehta hai 'connection to db-internal-7.corp:5432 refused'. Agar hum woh text forward kar dein, toh attacker ko hamari internal topology ka naksha mil gaya. Client ko bas itna jaanna hai: dependency down hai, try later (503), ya time par jawab nahi aaya (504).

Yeh mapping `src/adapters/http-status.ts` ke `mapResilienceError()` mein ek jagah hai, aur Express middleware aur NestJS filter dono isi ko use karte hain -- toh dono frameworks mein exact same body jaati hai. Comment literally kehta hai: 'The body never contains the dependency's error details (they may hold internal hostnames or tokens).'

Mutation A11 ('the error body leaks the dependency's message') 2 tests fail karta hai. Ek honest note: http-status.test.ts ka test sirf yeh check karta hai ki TimeoutError ke 1234 ms body mein na aaye; asli upstream body toh HttpError mein store hi nahi hota, isliye woh leak ho hi nahi sakta is path se.
why_needed: Error messages information disclosure ka common source hain (OWASP isko 'improper error handling' bolta hai). Gateway ki tarah behave karne wali service ko apne andar ki baatein andar hi rakhni chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Bank ka teller bolta hai 'server down hai, thodi der mein aaiye'. Woh aapko yeh nahi padh ke sunata ki core banking ke kaunse rack ka kaunsa disk fail hua.
how_it_works: mapResilienceError(error) instanceof se teen error classes pehchanta hai aur ek MappedError {status, headers, body} return karta hai jiski body hardcoded strings hain. error.message kabhi body mein copy nahi hota. Jo error map nahi hota uske liye undefined -- matlab adapter uska jawab hi nahi deta, framework deta hai.
in_this_project: src/adapters/http-status.ts: teen branches, har ek ki body constant. Express ka resilienceErrorHandler() aur Nest ka ResilienceExceptionFilter dono `res.end(JSON.stringify(mapped.body))` karte hain. HttpError ka constructor message 'upstream answered HTTP 401' jaisa hai -- usme sirf status hai, upstream ka response body nahi (test/support.ts ka getJson body ko `res.body?.cancel()` se chhod deta hai).
advantages: Internal details client tak nahi pahunchte
Express aur Nest dono mein ek jaisa response, ek hi jagah badalna
Client ke liye stable machine-readable `error` code
disadvantages: Debugging ke liye client-side par kam info; asli cause logs/onEvent se dekhna padega
Body English mein fixed hai, i18n nahi
common_mistakes: `err.message` seedha response mein bhej dena
Upstream ka response body error object mein store karke kahin log/forward kar dena bina redaction ke
Sochna ki 504 body mein timeout ms dena harmless hai -- yeh bhi internal config hai
follow_up_questions: Toh debugging ke liye asli error kahan jaata hai?
Agar product team chahti hai ki client ko kuch details milein toh kaise karoge bina leak kiye?
Express ka default handler development mode mein kya bhejta hai?

question: Why does HttpError carry upstreamStatus instead of status, and what security bug did that rename fix?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki Express ka default error handler (aur kai doosre) error object ka `err.status` padh ke wahi status code APNE client ko bhej deta hai. Pehle HttpError mein field ka naam `status` tha. Result: SMS provider ne 401 diya (hamari API key galat thi), aur Express ne hamare user ko 401 bhej diya -- matlab hamara client sochta hai ki WOH unauthorized hai, ki uska token expire ho gaya, aur shayad logout ho jaata hai. Upstream ka 404 hamare client ko lagta 'yeh route exist nahi karta'.

Yeh ek trust-boundary bug hai: dependency ki taraf ka status, jo hamare aur dependency ke beech ka maamla hai, bina soche client-facing contract ban gaya. Security angle: client ko galat auth signal milta hai, aur internal info (ki hum kis provider se baat kar rahe hain aur woh kya bol raha hai) leak hoti hai.

Yeh Express test ne pakda -- stage 3 mein rename hua. Ab field `upstreamStatus` hai, Express use nahi pehchanta, aur upstream error client tak plain 500 ban ke jaata hai, jab tak app jaan-bujh ke map na kare. Test 'an upstream 404 / 401 is NOT passed on as our status by Express's DEFAULT handler' dono cases check karta hai, aur Nest test bhi 'an upstream 401 is not passed on'. Mutation H1 (field wapas `status`) 3 tests fail karta hai.
why_needed: Dependency ka status code ek alag conversation ka hissa hai. Use apne API contract mein leak karna galat auth signals aur galat caching/redirect behaviour la sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Courier company ne aapke vendor ko bola 'address galat hai'. Vendor aapko yeh nahi bol sakta 'AAPKA address galat hai' -- galti vendor aur courier ke beech ki hai.
how_it_works: Express 4 ka finalhandler error se status nikalta hai `err.status` ya `err.statusCode` se (agar 4xx/5xx range mein ho). HttpError ab dono mein se koi field nahi rakhta, toh finalhandler 500 maan leta hai. isRetryableHttp bhi ab `error.upstreamStatus` padhta hai.
in_this_project: src/http.ts: `constructor(readonly upstreamStatus: number, readonly retryAfterMs: number | undefined)`, aur upar lamba comment jo bug ko explain karta hai. test/express.test.ts mein ek alag 'plain' Express app banti hai jisme sirf resilienceErrorHandler() hai, phir Express ka built-in handler; upstream 404 aur 401 dono par response 500 aata hai.
advantages: Upstream status kabhi accidentally client contract nahi banta
Mapping ab explicit decision hai (app chahe toh 502 ya 404 map kare)
Test real Express app se proof deta hai, assumption nahi
disadvantages: Public API field naam badla -- existing callers jo `e.status` padhte the unhe update karna pada
Har upstream failure ab default 500 hai, jo kabhi kabhi 502 se kam precise hai
common_mistakes: Error class par `status` ya `statusCode` naam ka field rakhna jab woh hamare client ke liye nahi hai
Sochna 'mera handler toh custom hai' -- koi bhi middleware ya framework default handler use padh sakta hai
Upstream 401 ko retry karna ya client ko forward karna
follow_up_questions: Agar tum upstream errors ko 502 Bad Gateway map karna chaho toh kahan karoge?
Kaun se aur libraries/frameworks err.status ya err.statusCode padhte hain?
Yeh bug unit test se kyun nahi pakda gaya, Express test se kyun?

question: A dependency sends Retry-After: 3600. Why is trusting Retry-After from another server risky, and how does the library limit it?
answer_hinglish:
Retry-After ek dusre server ki request hai, hukum nahi. Agar hum blindly maan lein, toh ek buggy ya compromised dependency 'Retry-After: 3600' bhej ke hamari har request ko ek ghante ke liye park kar sakti hai -- request handler, socket, memory, sab hold. Yeh ek tarah ka remote-controlled DoS hai hamare upar.

RetryPolicy mein iske liye `maxRetryAfterMs` hai, default 60 s. Logic: server jo delay maange, woh sirf tab use hota hai jab backoff se lamba ho (pehle retry karna bas ek aur 429 laata). Lekin agar maanga gaya delay maxRetryAfterMs se zyada hai, toh policy wait nahi karti -- seedha give up karti hai reason `retry-after-too-long` ke saath, aur last error unchanged rethrow karti hai. Matlab hum server ki baat ka respect karte hain (pehle retry nahi karte), lekin apni request ko ghante bhar latkate bhi nahi.

Parsing bhi defensive hai: `parseRetryAfter()` sirf pure digits ya ek HTTP-date maanta hai; `-5`, `1.5`, `soon`, khaali string -> undefined (ignore). Past date -> 0. Mutation R22 (cap ignore) aur R31 (`-5`, `1.5` as dates) dono tests se pakde gaye.

Ek aur layer: retry ka `deadlineMs` -- agar Retry-After deadline ke baad retry start karwata, toh `deadline` reason se give up.
why_needed: Remote server ke numbers ko apne resources control karne dena trust boundary todna hai. Cap ke bina ek header aapke saare workers ko sula sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Dukaandaar bolta hai 'kal aana'. Aap kal tak dukaan ke bahar khade nahi rehte; aap ghar jaate ho aur baad mein decide karte ho.
how_it_works: retry.ts: `asked = o.retryAfterMs?.(error)`; agar NaN nahi aur backoff delay se bada (Infinity bhi 'bada' hai) -> agar `asked > (o.maxRetryAfterMs ?? 60_000)` toh giveUp('retry-after-too-long'), warna `delayMs = Math.ceil(asked)`. Uske baad deadline check. Phir cancellable sleep.
in_this_project: src/retry.ts mein ye check; src/http.ts ka parseRetryAfter() regex `^\d+$` (seconds) ya Date.parse (letters hone par). http.test.ts real loopback server se '429 + Retry-After: 1' bhejta hai aur policy exactly 1000 ms wait record karti hai. Ek edge jo interview bank likhte waqt mila (README F4): 400-digit ka Retry-After `Number()` mein Infinity ban jaata hai, aur pehle retry.ts `Number.isFinite(asked)` check par use IGNORE karke normal backoff se retry karta tha -- jabki 3600 par give up karta. Ab check `!Number.isNaN(asked)` hai: Infinity 'too long' gina jaata hai aur give up `retry-after-too-long`; sirf NaN ignore hota hai. Test retry.test.ts 'an absurdly long Retry-After (Infinity, e.g. 400 digits) gives up too; NaN is ignored', mutation F4.
advantages: Server ki baat maani jaati hai jab woh reasonable ho
Ek header se request ghanton park nahi ho sakti
Give-up reason alag hai, toh metrics mein dikh jaata hai
disadvantages: 60 s default bhi ek HTTP request ke liye bahut lamba ho sakta hai -- app ko apni incoming timeout ke hisaab se kam karna chahiye
Retry-After ko shorter backoff override nahi karta (by design), toh server 'Retry-After: 0' bole toh bhi hamara backoff chalega
common_mistakes: Retry-After ko as-is setTimeout mein daal dena
Seconds ko ms samajh lena (mutation R29)
Negative ya decimal values accept karna
follow_up_questions: maxRetryAfterMs ko incoming request ke timeout se kaise relate karoge?
Worker/queue job ke liye kya tum 3600 maan loge?
Retry-After ko breaker ke openMs se kaise jod sakte ho?

question: npm audit warns about multer in this project. Is the library vulnerable, and how do you reason about it?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha jawab: library ke shipped code mein multer nahi hai. Warning dev dependency se aati hai. `@nestjs/platform-express` 10.x sirf tests ke liye install hai (taaki ek real NestJS 10 app chala ke adapter test ho sake), aur woh multer 1.x kheench laata hai, jise npm deprecated aur known vulnerabilities wala bata raha hai. README ki 'NOT implemented' list mein yeh honestly likha hai: 'nothing here uses multer and none of it is shipped.'

Reasoning kaise karte hain: pehle dekho package runtime mein kya laata hai. package.json mein `dependencies` hai hi nahi -- zero runtime dependencies. `@nestjs/common` ek optional peer dependency hai (`peerDependenciesMeta` mein `optional: true`), matlab user ki apni Nest app jo version laaye, wahi use hota hai; core aur Express entry use bilkul import nahi karte. Baaki sab -- express, @nestjs/core, platform-express, cockatiel, vitest -- `devDependencies` hain.

Phir dekho vulnerable code path reachable hai ya nahi: multer file upload parse karta hai; hamare tests koi multipart upload nahi karte. Toh risk developer machine/CI tak hai, production tak nahi.

Lekin ignore bhi mat karo: CI mein noisy audit asli warnings ko chhupa deta hai. Sahi next step hai platform-express ka newer major (jab test kiya jaaye) ya audit ko `--omit=dev` se production deps par chalana.
why_needed: Supply chain security mein sabse pehla sawaal hota hai: yeh code production mein jaata hai ya nahi. Dev aur runtime dependency ka fark samajhna zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Construction site par contractor ki ek purani seedhi kharab hai. Ghar ke andar woh seedhi nahi rehti -- lekin jab tak site chal rahi hai, mazdoor ke liye risk hai.
how_it_works: npm devDependencies sirf `npm ci`/`npm install` par repo ke andar aati hain; jab koi package ko dependency ki tarah install karta hai toh devDependencies nahi aati. Optional peer dependency ka matlab: host app provide kare toh use, warna install warning nahi.
in_this_project: package.json: koi `dependencies` block nahi; `peerDependencies: { "@nestjs/common": ">=10" }` aur `peerDependenciesMeta` mein optional. Dev deps exact pinned versions hain (express 4.21.2, @nestjs/* 10.4.15, cockatiel 3.2.1). src/index.ts comment: 'Core entry point: no framework, no runtime dependency.' Package `private: true` hai aur npm par published nahi.
advantages: Zero runtime deps: supply-chain surface minimal
Exact pinned dev versions: tests reproducible
Limitation README mein khule aam likhi hai
disadvantages: Dev machine/CI par vulnerable package phir bhi install hota hai
Audit noise asli issues chhupa sakta hai
common_mistakes: Har npm audit warning ko production risk maan lena (ya ulta, sabko ignore karna)
Framework ko hard dependency bana dena jisse har user ko woh install karna pade
Optional peer dep ko normal dependency mein daal dena
follow_up_questions: `npm audit --omit=dev` aur normal audit mein kya fark hai?
Agar yeh library publish hoti toh tum kaunse supply-chain checks lagate?
Optional peer dependency ka downside kya hai -- version mismatch?

question: How can retries turn your own service into a DoS attack on a dependency, and which parts of this library defend against it?
answer_hinglish:
Retry ek innocent feature lagta hai, lekin outage ke waqt yeh load multiply karta hai -- exactly tab jab dependency sabse kamzor hai. 3 attempts per call matlab down dependency ko 3x traffic. Agar teen layers har ek 3 baar retry karein (gateway -> service -> client), toh budget.ts ka comment kehta hai: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27x. Yeh self-inflicted DoS hai -- 'retry storm' -- aur recovery ko bhi rokta hai kyunki jaise hi dependency uthti hai, jama hua traffic use phir gira deta hai.

Is library mein defenses layers mein hain:
1. RetryBudget (gRPC retry throttling): har failure -1 token, har success +0.1, retry sirf tab jab tokens > half. Measured simulation: 1000 calls x 3 attempts down dependency par -- bina budget 3000 attempts, default budget ke saath 1003. Real sockets par 20 calls closed port par 23 attempts.
2. Full jitter default: saare clients ek saath wapas nahi aate.
3. shouldRetry: 4xx retry nahi (isRetryableHttp), aur non-retryable errors budget ko touch nahi karte.
4. Circuit breaker retry ke andar: open hone par BrokenCircuitError, aur isRetryableHttp usko retry nahi karta (mutation K9) -- toh 0 retries.
5. maxRetryAfterMs aur deadlineMs.

Lekin jo library nahi kar sakti: tumhare doosre layers ka retry. Yeh design rule hai -- retry ek hi layer par karo.
why_needed: Availability bhi security ka hissa hai (CIA ka A). Apni hi retries se dependency ko girana ek classic incident pattern hai.
real_world_analogy: Bijli jaane par sab ek saath AC on rakhte hain; bijli aate hi poora mohalla ek saath load daalta hai aur transformer phir ud jaata hai. Budget = 'pehle kuch ghar on karo, baaki baad mein'.
how_it_works: RetryBudget tokens thousandths mein count karta hai (no float drift). retry.ts: shouldRetry false -> give up bina budget change; warna budget.onFailure(), phir attempts check, phir `!budget.canRetry()` -> give up 'budget'. Success par onSuccess(). Budget ek dependency ke saare calls mein shared hota hai, isliye sustained outage mein jaldi drain hota hai.
in_this_project: src/budget.ts (RetryBudget, comment mein 27x example), src/retry.ts give-up order, src/http.ts isRetryableHttp. README 'Retry storm' table: no budget 3000, with budget 1003 (3 + 2 + 998 x 1). Recovery: 51 successes ke baad canRetry() true, 72 total ke baad ek single failure phir retry hota hai.
advantages: Outage mein retries khud band, recovery par khud wapas
Breaker ke saath zero load during open
Measured numbers se proof
disadvantages: Budget per process hai -- N replicas ke N budgets
Budget ke baad bhi har call ka ek attempt jaata hai (1003, 1000 nahi)
Doosri layers ke retries par control nahi
common_mistakes: Har layer par retry lagana
Budget har call ke liye naya `new RetryBudget()` banana (kabhi drain nahi hoga)
Breaker rejection ko retry karna
follow_up_questions: Budget per process hai -- 10 replicas mein total amplification kya hoga?
Retry sirf ek layer par -- kaunsi layer, aur kyun?
Hedged requests isse kaise alag hain?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Budget ratio-based hai, isliye fixed rate-limit se better adapt karta hai, lekin pehle kuch failures tak har call 3 attempts karta hai (shuru ke 3 + 2). Breaker load ko zero karta hai, budget load ko ~1x par rakhta hai -- dono saath chahiye.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Budget har call ke liye naya bana diya -> kabhi drain nahi hota, storm wapas. shouldRetry na diya -> default 'always', 400s bhi retry. Breaker retry ke bahar -> 4 outcomes, breaker band hi rehta hai (wrap.test.ts).
advanced.alternatives: Fixed max-retries-per-second, adaptive concurrency (implement nahi), server-side load shedding, client-side rate limiting.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10 replicas mein har ek ka budget alag; budget ratio-based hai, toh har replica apne andar retries ko limit karta hai aur total amplification replicas ke saath multiply nahi hota jaisa fixed count mein hota -- lekin har replica ko apna bucket drain karna padta hai, aur shared budget nahi hai (README: anything shared between processes is not built). Is per-replica behaviour ka koi measurement repo mein nahi hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Give-up reason 'budget' par alert; budget.available ko gauge metric banao; upstream se Retry-After respect karo; retry sirf edge layer par.

question: What does loadShedding protect against for incoming requests, and what does it NOT protect against?
answer_hinglish:
loadShedding(bulkhead) ek Express middleware hai jo INCOMING requests par concurrency cap lagata hai: maxConcurrent tak requests handle hoti hain, maxQueue tak wait karti hain, baaki ko turant 503 `{"error":"overloaded"}` aur `Retry-After: 1`. Iska fayda: traffic spike ya ek slow downstream ke waqt requests pile up hoke har request ko slow nahi karti; jo serve ho sakti hain woh fast serve hoti hain, baaki fail fast. Yeh availability defense hai -- overload ke against.

Kya protect NAHI karta:
1. Per-client fairness nahi hai. Ek abusive client saare slots bhar sakta hai aur genuine users ko 503 milega. Yeh rate limiter nahi hai (per IP/per key limit nahi).
2. Sirf wahi route protect hota hai jahan middleware laga hai (README example: `/heavy`).
3. Per process hai -- 3 replicas = 3 alag caps.
4. Network-level flood (SYN flood, slowloris before handler) Express tak pahunchne se pehle ka maamla hai.

Ek achhi detail: slot response finish hone ya connection close hone tak hold hota hai, toh client disconnect par slot free hota hai (mutation A8 test se pakda). Test: Bulkhead maxConcurrent 2, maxQueue 0 -- teesri concurrent request ko 503 overloaded milta hai, aur pehli finish hone ke baad naya request andar aata hai.
why_needed: Bina cap ke overload mein latency sab requests ke liye badhti hai (queueing), timeouts cascade karte hain, aur memory badhti hai. Fail-fast 503 better hai bajaye sabko slow karne ke.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant mein 20 table hain. 21va group ko 'abhi jagah nahi, 10 min baad aaiye' bolna better hai bajaye sabko khade-khade aadha khana dene ke. Lekin bouncer yeh nahi dekhta ki ek hi aadmi 15 table book kar raha hai.
how_it_works: shedLoad() bulkhead.execute() ko ek operation deta hai jo promise banata hai, `res.once('close')` par resolve hota hai, aur `next()` bula deta hai. Toh slot tab tak busy jab tak response close na ho. Rejection par BulkheadRejectedError -> resilienceErrorHandler() se 503. Queue mein wait karte hue client chala gaya -> ClientClosedError, kuch nahi bheja jaata.
in_this_project: src/adapters/express.ts loadShedding(). test/express.test.ts: 'loadShedding: 2 slots; the 3rd concurrent request gets 503 at once; a finished request frees its slot' aur 'a client that disconnects mid-request frees its slot'. Mapping http-status.ts mein: bulkhead -> 503 + retry-after '1'.
code_example:
// real, README.md usage
app.use("/heavy", loadShedding(new Bulkhead({ maxConcurrent: 50 }))); // at most 50 requests in flight, else 503
advantages: Overload mein fast fail, tail latency control
Disconnect par slot free
Same Bulkhead class, koi naya concept nahi
disadvantages: Per-client fairness nahi
Retry-After hamesha 1 -- spike lamba ho toh clients jaldi lautenge
Process-local cap
common_mistakes: loadShedding ko rate limiter samajhna
Saare routes par ek hi tiny bulkhead laga dena (health check bhi 503)
maxQueue bahut bada rakhna -- phir yeh shedding nahi, sirf ek lambi line hai
follow_up_questions: Per-client limit chahiye toh kya add karoge?
Health check endpoint ko loadShedding ke peeche rakhoge?
maxQueue > 0 kab useful hai?

question: Why does resilienceErrorHandler pass unknown errors to next() instead of answering them, and how would you design error handling at this trust boundary in a real API?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki middleware sirf woh errors map karta hai jinka matlab woh confidently jaanta hai: BrokenCircuitError -> 503 + Retry-After, BulkheadRejectedError -> 503, TimeoutError -> 504. Baaki sab -- validation error, auth error, HttpError, bug -- app ka maamla hai. Agar middleware sab kuch khud answer kar deta, toh app ka apna error handler (jo shayad logging, error tracking, correct 400/401 karta hai) kabhi chalta hi nahi, aur ek library app ki error policy ko override kar deti. Mutation A4 ('the error handler answers unknown errors itself instead of next()') ko test 'errors it does not map reach the app's own error handler unchanged' pakadta hai -- woh check karta hai ki HttpError aur plain Error dono same object ke roop mein app ke handler tak pahunchein.

Trust boundary design (real API mein, library ke bahar):
1. Upstream error kabhi as-is client tak nahi -- isiliye upstreamStatus rename.
2. Ek last-resort app handler jo hamesha generic 500 + correlation id bhejta hai, aur full error sirf logs mein.
3. Jaan-bujh ke mapping: upstream 5xx -> 502, upstream 404 shayad hamara 404 (agar semantically same resource hai) -- yeh decision app ka.
4. Express ka built-in handler production mein mat chhodo: non-production env mein woh stack trace bhejta hai (general Express behaviour, library ka code nahi).

Library ka hissa chhota aur predictable hai -- yahi iski strength hai.
why_needed: Ek library jo saare errors nigal leti hai, app ki observability aur correctness dono tod deti hai. Boundary par explicit mapping hi safe hai.
real_world_analogy: Reception desk sirf woh sawaal answer karta hai jo uski list mein hain ('lift kharab hai, 5 min'); baaki sawaal manager ke paas bhejta hai -- khud se kuch bhi jawab nahi ghadta.
how_it_works: resilienceErrors(error, req, res, next): mapped = mapResilienceError(error); agar undefined ya res.headersSent -> next(error) aur return. Warna status, headers, JSON body. Express error middleware 4 arguments se pehchanta hai, isliye function ka signature 4-arity hai.
in_this_project: src/adapters/express.ts. NestJS mein same idea `@Catch(BrokenCircuitError, BulkheadRejectedError, TimeoutError)` se -- filter sirf in teen ko pakadta hai, baaki Nest ki own handling (test: 'other errors keep Nest's own 500', body `{statusCode: 500, message: 'Internal server error'}`).
advantages: App ki error policy intact
Library ka behaviour chhota aur testable
Express aur Nest mein same contract
disadvantages: App ko phir bhi ek safe last-resort handler likhna padega -- library nahi deti
Upstream errors default 500, 502 nahi
common_mistakes: Error middleware routes se pehle register karna
Middleware ko 3 arguments ka bana dena (Express use normal middleware samjhega)
Har error ko 500 + err.message bhejna
follow_up_questions: Upstream 5xx ko 502 map karne ka middleware likho
Correlation id client ko dena aur logs mein kaise jodoge?
Nest mein @Catch() bina arguments ke lagaoge toh kya hoga?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Narrow mapping (sirf 3 classes) predictable hai lekin app ko baaki khud karna padta hai. Broad mapping convenient lagti hai lekin app ke decisions override karti hai aur galat status bhej sakti hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Middleware routes se pehle laga -> kabhi call nahi hota. App ka koi handler nahi -> Express default handler, jo dev mode mein stack dikhata hai. Error classes do copies mein load -> instanceof fail -> 503 ki jagah 500.
advanced.alternatives: Ek central error-mapping table (error class -> status) app level par; RFC 7807 problem+json bodies; API gateway par error normalisation.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Zyada dependencies ke saath har ek ka alag error code chahiye ho sakta hai (dependency naam bina leak kiye) -- body mein stable `error` code + correlation id scale karta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Last-resort handler with correlation id, upstream 5xx -> 502 mapping, structured logs with error class aur policy name (onEvent se).

question: If you wrap a database query in TimeoutPolicy, does the query actually stop on the database server?
answer_hinglish:
Depends karta hai driver par -- aur yeh library ke haath mein nahi hai. Pehle clear: is project mein DB nahi hai; yeh library kisi bhi async call ko wrap karti hai, aur README DB driver ko ek example ki tarah mention karta hai ('Pass the signal on to whatever does the work (fetch, a driver)').

TimeoutPolicy timeout par do kaam karta hai: (1) operation ko diya gaya AbortSignal abort karta hai, reason TimeoutError, aur (2) turant TimeoutError se reject karta hai, chahe operation signal ignore kare. Toh caller ko hamesha time par jawab milta hai. Lekin query ruki ya nahi, yeh is par depend karta hai ki tumhara driver signal sunta hai ya nahi. Agar driver signal accept karta hai aur abort par query cancel karta hai, toh DB par bhi kaam rukta hai. Agar driver signal ignore karta hai, toh promise reject ho gaya lekin query DB par chal rahi hai, connection pool ka connection busy hai, aur locks pakde hue hain.

Isliye production mein DB ke liye do layers chahiye: client-side TimeoutPolicy (caller ko jaldi jawab) aur server-side timeout (jaise Postgres ka statement_timeout) jo DB khud enforce kare. HTTP ke liye library ne yeh prove kiya hai: hanging server test mein server ko connection close dikhta hai. DB ke liye aisa koi test nahi hai.
why_needed: Sirf promise reject karna 'waiting band karna' hai, 'kaam band karna' nahi. DB mein bhaagti hui query connections aur locks khaati rehti hai.
real_world_analogy: Aapne waiter ko bola 'order cancel'. Agar waiter kitchen tak message nahi le jaata, toh chef phir bhi khana bana raha hai -- aapka table khaali hai lekin gas jal rahi hai.
how_it_works: TimeoutPolicy ek naya AbortController banata hai, caller ka signal usme link karta hai, setTimeout par `controller.abort(new TimeoutError(ms))`, aur `Promise.race([operation(controller.signal), stopped])`. finally mein timer clear aur caller listener remove.
in_this_project: src/timeout.ts ka comment: 'so a well-behaved operation (fetch, a DB driver that takes a signal) really stops instead of running on in the background'. Test 'rejects on timeout even if the operation ignores its signal' prove karta hai ki caller ko jawab milta hai -- lekin uska matlab yahi hai ki signal ignore karne wala operation background mein chalta reh sakta hai.
advantages: Caller ko guaranteed time par jawab
Signal-aware driver ke saath asli cancellation
Ek hi Operation shape -- fetch aur DB dono
disadvantages: Signal ignore karne wala driver background mein kaam karta rehta hai
Client aur server timeouts ko alag-alag tune karna padta hai
common_mistakes: Maan lena ki promise reject = query cancel
Server-side statement timeout na lagana
Client timeout ko DB timeout se chhota rakhna bina soche -- caller retry karega jabki pehli query abhi bhi chal rahi hai

Client timeout aur statement_timeout mein kaunsa bada hona chahiye?

question: Can you use isRetryableHttp as shouldRetry for database calls? Which DB errors should you retry?
answer_hinglish:
Nahi -- aur yeh ek subtle trap hai. Pehle: is project mein DB nahi hai, aur isRetryableHttp HTTP ke liye bana hai. Uska rule hai: agar error HttpError nahi hai toh `true` (maan leta hai ki network error ya timeout hai). Ab DB errors HttpError nahi hote -- toh unique constraint violation, syntax error, foreign key violation, permission denied, sab 'retryable' ban jaayenge. Matlab ek duplicate-key insert 3 baar fail hoga, budget drain karega, aur breaker (agar isFailure bhi wahi hai) ise dependency down samjhega.

DB ke liye apna shouldRetry likho. Generic rule:
- Retry: connection refused/reset, timeout (TimeoutError), deadlock aur serialization failure (lekin poora transaction retry, single statement nahi), 'too many connections' type transient errors, failover ke dauraan read-only/primary-gone errors.
- Retry mat karo: constraint violations, syntax/permission errors, data errors -- yeh har baar same fail honge.

isFailure bhi alag socho: constraint violation DB ka sahi jawab hai (DB healthy hai), toh woh breaker ke liye success hona chahiye -- breaker.ts ka design yahi kehta hai: 'A 404 or a validation error is the dependency answering correctly: return false and it counts as a SUCCESS'.

Library yeh flexibility deti hai kyunki shouldRetry aur isFailure plain functions hain.
why_needed: Galat classification retries ko bekaar load mein, aur breaker ko false alarm mein badal deti hai. HTTP helper ko blindly DB par lagana yahi karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Doctor 'bukhar' (transient) ke liye kal phir bulata hai, lekin 'tooti haddi' (permanent) ke liye kal phir aane se haddi nahi judti.
how_it_works: retry.ts: `if (o.shouldRetry !== undefined && !o.shouldRetry(error, attempt)) giveUp('not-retryable')` -- non-retryable error budget ko touch nahi karta. breaker.ts: `isFailure(error)` false -> outcome 'success'. Dono functions caller ki marzi.
in_this_project: src/http.ts isRetryableHttp: `if (!(error instanceof HttpError)) return true;`. http.test.ts mein `new TypeError('fetch failed')` aur TimeoutError dono retryable. RetryOptions comment: 'say no to errors that will not change (HTTP 400/401/403/404/422, validation errors)'.
advantages: shouldRetry/isFailure pluggable hain -- DB ke liye alag likh sakte ho
Non-retryable errors budget nahi khaate
disadvantages: Library DB classifier nahi deti -- har driver ke error codes alag
Galat default (always retry) agar shouldRetry na diya
common_mistakes: isRetryableHttp ko DB par use karna
Deadlock par sirf failed statement retry karna (transaction pehle hi rollback ho chuka)
Constraint violation ko breaker failure ginna
follow_up_questions: Serialization failure par retry kahan karoge -- query level ya transaction level?
isFailure aur shouldRetry kab alag hone chahiye?
Failover ke dauraan kaunse errors aate hain?

question: How would you organise these policies around a data-access layer: one policy per query, per repository, or per database?
answer_hinglish:
Rule README se: 'One set of policies PER DEPENDENCY, created once (module level / a singleton service), shared by every call.' DB ke liye (is project mein DB nahi hai, yeh design guidance hai) iska matlab: ek database (ya ek cluster endpoint) = ek dependency = ek breaker, ek retry budget. Kyunki breaker aur budget ka poora point hai saare calls ka aggregate health dekhna. Har query ke liye naya CircuitBreaker banaoge toh har breaker ke paas 1-2 outcomes honge, minimumCalls (default 10) kabhi poore nahi honge, aur breaker kabhi nahi khulega. Har call ke liye naya RetryBudget kabhi drain nahi hoga.

Lekin bulkhead ke liye alag sochna pad sakta hai. Agar ek hi DB par fast lookups aur slow reports dono chalte hain, toh ek slow report query saare slots kha sakti hai. Tab do bulkheads -- 'db-oltp' aur 'db-reports' -- taaki reports OLTP ko starve na karein. Yeh bulkhead ka original idea hai: ek compartment doobe toh poora jahaz na doobe.

Practical layout: ek `db.ts` module jo per-database breaker + budget + do bulkheads export kare, aur repository functions unhe wrap() se compose karein. NestJS mein yeh ek singleton provider. Har policy ko `name` do ('orders-db-breaker') taaki onEvent metrics alag dikhein.
why_needed: Breaker aur budget statistics hain -- unhe kaafi data chahiye. Galat granularity unhe bekaar ya kabhi trigger na hone wala bana deti hai.
real_world_analogy: Society mein ek main water valve per building hota hai (breaker), har nal par nahi. Lekin garden ki pipe ka alag valve hota hai taaki garden ka leak ghar ka paani na khaaye (alag bulkhead).
how_it_works: CircuitBreaker count-based ring buffer rakhta hai (windowSize 20, minimumCalls 10 defaults). Bulkhead ka `active` counter aur FIFO queue instance par hai. Isliye sharing instance share karne se hota hai -- koi global registry nahi hai.
in_this_project: README ka sms example: module level par `const sms = wrap(...)` aur har sendSms() call usi ko use karti hai. Policies ke `name` options ('sms-retry', 'sms-breaker', 'sms-pool', 'sms-timeout') events mein `policy` field ban jaate hain. Library mein koi registry/keyed policy map nahi hai -- woh app banata hai.
advantages: Breaker/budget ko enough data milta hai
Slow workloads isolated
Names se metrics alag
disadvantages: Shared breaker: ek bad query class poore DB ka breaker khol sakti hai
App ko khud wiring/registry likhni padti hai
common_mistakes: Har request mein `new CircuitBreaker()`
Ek bulkhead saare workloads ke liye
Policies ko naam na dena -- metrics mein sab 'breaker'
follow_up_questions: Ek slow query poore DB breaker ko khol de toh?
Read replica aur primary ke liye alag breakers?
NestJS mein ise provider kaise banaoge?

question: A write times out and RetryPolicy retries it. How can that create duplicate rows, and how would you make it safe?
answer_hinglish:
Timeout ka matlab 'mujhe pata nahi', 'fail hua' nahi. Pehle: is project mein DB nahi hai -- yeh policies ko DB write ke around lagane ka sawaal hai. Scenario: INSERT order bheja, DB ne commit kar diya, lekin ack aane se pehle TimeoutPolicy ne 2 s par abort kar diya. Caller ko TimeoutError mila. isRetryableHttp TimeoutError ko retryable maanta hai, toh RetryPolicy dobara INSERT bhejta hai -- ab do orders. Payment ya SMS ho toh do charges / do messages.

Yeh library is problem ko solve nahi karti -- RetryPolicy ko nahi pata operation idempotent hai ya nahi. Yeh caller ki zimmedari hai. Options:
1. Non-idempotent writes par retry hi mat karo: `shouldRetry` mein write ke liye false, ya writes ke liye maxAttempts 1.
2. Idempotency key: operation ke BAHAR ek key banao (har attempt mein same), aur DB mein unique constraint. Dusra attempt constraint violation dega -> use 'already done' maano aur existing row padho. Important: key retry ke bahar banni chahiye, operation ke andar nahi -- warna har attempt nayi key.
3. Upsert / `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` jaise naturally idempotent statements.
4. Timeout ke baad pehle 'check status' query, phir decide.

Yahi reason hai ki README kehta hai 'say no to errors that will not change' -- lekin timeout 'change ho sakta hai' wala error hai, isliye default classification yahan dangerous hai.
why_needed: At-least-once delivery + non-idempotent operation = duplicates. Retry library sirf at-least-once deti hai; exactly-once effect app ko banana padta hai.
real_world_analogy: Aapne dost ko UPI kiya, app spinning par atak gaya. Aap phir se bhej doge toh shayad do baar paise chale gaye. Samajhdaar app pehle 'transaction status' check karta hai.
how_it_works: RetryPolicy loop: har failure par shouldRetry, budget, attempts, Retry-After, deadline check, phir sleep aur dobara `operation(signal)`. Operation closure same rehta hai -- toh agar closure ke bahar idempotency key banao toh har attempt mein same key jaati hai.
in_this_project: src/retry.ts mein koi idempotency concept nahi hai. src/http.ts isRetryableHttp TimeoutError par true deta hai (http.test.ts: 'network errors and timeouts are retryable'). README ka sms example POST ko retry karta hai -- wahan bhi provider-side idempotency ki zaroorat hogi, library yeh document nahi karti.
advantages: Idempotency key ke saath retries safe ho jaate hain
Library generic rehti hai -- reads aur writes dono wrap kar sakti hai
disadvantages: Library warn nahi karti ki operation non-idempotent hai
Idempotency key ke liye schema change aur cleanup chahiye
common_mistakes: Timeout ko 'failed' samajhna
Idempotency key operation ke andar banana
Writes par wahi retry policy lagana jo reads par
follow_up_questions: Idempotency keys kab expire karoge?
Transaction ke beech timeout ho toh commit hua ya nahi kaise pata karoge?
Payment provider idempotency key support na kare toh?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Writes par retry band karna simple aur safe hai lekin transient failures user tak pahunchte hain. Idempotency key se retries safe hote hain lekin schema aur storage cost.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Commit hua par ack lost -> retry -> duplicate. Key andar bani -> har attempt alag key -> duplicate phir bhi. Unique constraint violation ko 'error' maan ke user ko fail dikhana jabki pehla attempt successful tha.
advanced.alternatives: Outbox pattern, ON CONFLICT upserts, provider-side idempotency keys, status-check-then-retry.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Zyada traffic par idempotency table badhti hai -- TTL/partitioning chahiye. Retry budget phir bhi zaroori, kyunki safe retry bhi load hai.
advanced.production_improvements: shouldRetry ko operation type ke hisaab se alag karo (read vs write), idempotency key har write par, give-up events par 'timeout on write' alag metric.

question: How should a Bulkhead's maxConcurrent relate to the database connection pool size?
answer_hinglish:
Short answer: bulkhead maxConcurrent pool size se zyada nahi hona chahiye, aur aksar thoda kam. Pehle: is project mein DB ya connection pool nahi hai; Bulkhead ek generic concurrency limiter hai, aur yeh question use DB ke saamne lagane ka hai.

Agar pool 10 connections ka hai aur bulkhead 50 allow karta hai, toh 40 calls bulkhead se paas ho ke pool ki internal queue mein wait karengi. Ab do queues hain: bulkhead ki (jo bounded hai, cancellable hai, events deti hai) aur pool ki (jo shayad unbounded hai aur jiska wait TimeoutPolicy ke andar count hota hai). Result: requests pool mein wait karte hue timeout hoti hain, aur timeout ka matlab galat lagta hai -- 'DB slow hai' jabki DB idle hai, bas pool full hai. Breaker bhi in timeouts ko failure gin ke khul sakta hai.

Agar bulkhead = pool size (ya thoda kam, kuch connections migrations/health checks ke liye), toh waiting sirf bulkhead mein hoti hai, jo FIFO hai, maxQueue se bounded hai, aur caller abort par queue chhod deta hai. Excess calls turant BulkheadRejectedError -- fast 503.

Yaad rakho: Bulkhead per process hai. 4 replicas x pool 10 = 40 DB connections -- DB ka max_connections isse upar hona chahiye. Concurrency ka andaaza Little's law se (generic): concurrency ~ throughput x latency.
why_needed: Do stacked queues mein se ek invisible ho toh latency aur timeouts ka diagnosis galat hota hai. Limit wahi lagao jahan observe aur control kar sako.
real_world_analogy: Petrol pump par 10 nozzles hain. Gate par guard 50 gaadiyan andar aane deta hai -- andar jam lagta hai aur koi nahi nikal pata. Guard ko 10 (plus thodi line) hi andar aane deni chahiye.
how_it_works: Bulkhead: `active < maxConcurrent` -> run; warna `queue.length < maxQueue` -> waitForSlot (FIFO, abortable); warna reject. Release slot ko seedha agle waiter ko hand off karta hai (no barging). TimeoutPolicy bulkhead ke ANDAR (recommended order), toh timeout sirf actual call ka hota hai, bulkhead queue ka wait nahi.
in_this_project: src/bulkhead.ts. wrap.ts comment: 'bulkhead outside timeout: a slot is held at most for one attempt's timeout, never during the retry's backoff sleep'. http.test.ts: hanging server ke saamne maxConcurrent 2 -- 6 calls mein se 2 server tak pahunchte hain aur timeout hote hain, 4 turant refuse. `running` aur `queued` getters metrics ke liye.
advantages: Ek hi visible, bounded, cancellable queue
Timeouts asli DB latency dikhate hain, pool wait nahi
Fast rejection jab capacity full
disadvantages: Pool aur bulkhead config sync mein rakhna padta hai
Per-process limit: cluster-wide connections ka hisaab manually
common_mistakes: Bulkhead pool se bada
Timeout ko bulkhead ke bahar rakhna -- queue wait bhi timeout mein gin jaata hai
Replicas ka multiplication bhool jaana
follow_up_questions: Pool ke andar ki queue ko timeout kaise karoge?
Autoscaling ke saath DB max_connections kaise bachaoge?
Bulkhead full hone par 503 dena sahi hai ya queue karna?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Bulkhead == pool: clean, lekin pool ke andar migrations/health checks ke liye jagah nahi. Bulkhead < pool: thodi headroom, thodi capacity waste.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Pool exhaustion bulkhead ke bina -> hidden queue -> timeouts -> breaker false open. Bulkhead queue bahut badi -> latency badhti hai bina fail-fast ke.
advanced.alternatives: Pool ka apna acquire-timeout, PgBouncer jaisa external pooler, adaptive concurrency (is library mein implement nahi).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x replicas par per-process pool x replicas DB ki limit cross kar sakta hai -- external pooler ya per-replica pool chhota karna padega; bulkhead bhi uske saath ghatega.
advanced.production_improvements: running/queued gauges, bulkhead-rejected events par alert, pool metrics ke saath ek dashboard par.

question: How would you apply timeouts, retries and a deadline to a multi-statement database transaction using this library?
answer_hinglish:
Key idea: retry aur deadline TRANSACTION ke level par, timeout har STATEMENT ya poore transaction par -- aur kabhi bhi transaction ke beech se ek statement retry nahi. Pehle: is project mein DB nahi hai; yeh library ke primitives ka DB par design hai.

Kyun statement-level retry galat hai: agar transaction ka teesra statement deadlock se fail hua, toh DB poora transaction rollback kar chuka hota hai. Sirf teesra statement dobara chalana pehle do ke bina hoga -- data inconsistent. Isliye Operation = 'BEGIN ... COMMIT poora', aur RetryPolicy us poore operation ko retry karta hai (shouldRetry sirf deadlock/serialization/connection errors par true).

Deadline: RetryPolicy ka `deadlineMs` total time limit hai, lekin dhyan do -- README: 'no retry that would START after this much total time'. Yaani ek attempt deadline se thoda pehle start hua toh woh deadline ke baad tak chal sakta hai. Isliye TimeoutPolicy bhi andar rakho: worst case approx deadlineMs + ek attempt ka timeout.

Abort par cleanup: TimeoutPolicy signal abort karta hai. Operation ko signal par ROLLBACK karna chahiye aur connection pool ko wapas dena chahiye -- library yeh nahi karti, operation karta hai. Caller ka signal (requestSignal) bhi isme link hota hai, toh client chala gaya toh transaction bhi cancel.

Commit ke dauraan timeout = ambiguous (commit hua ya nahi) -- idempotency wala sawaal.
why_needed: Transactions all-or-nothing hain; resilience policies ko bhi us unit ko respect karna chahiye, warna partial work ya duplicate work hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Ghar shift karte waqt truck beech raste kharab ho gaya. Aap aadha saamaan dobara nahi bhejte -- poora load wapas aata hai aur poori trip dobara.
how_it_works: wrap(retry, breaker, bulkhead, timeout): retry outermost loop, har attempt ko naya TimeoutPolicy AbortController. deadline check: `now() + delayMs - startedAt >= deadlineMs` -> giveUp('deadline'). Caller abort par retry turant ruk jaata hai aur backoff sleep bhi cancel.
in_this_project: src/retry.ts deadlineMs logic; src/timeout.ts per-attempt abort; wrap.test.ts 'timeout INSIDE retry: every attempt gets its own deadline' aur 'timeout OUTSIDE retry: one deadline for all attempts and waits (the third attempt never happens)'.
advantages: Transaction atomicity respect hoti hai
Client disconnect par transaction bhi cancel
Deadline se total time bounded
disadvantages: Rollback/cleanup operation ko khud likhna padta hai
deadlineMs soft hai -- last attempt ke timeout jitna overshoot
Commit-time timeout ambiguous
common_mistakes: Single statement retry karna transaction ke andar
Abort par ROLLBACK aur connection release bhoolna
deadlineMs ko hard limit samajhna
follow_up_questions: Commit ke dauraan timeout ho toh kya karoge?
Long transaction ko breaker failure ginna chahiye?
Serialization failures ke liye kitne attempts?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Transaction-level retry correct hai lekin mehnga (poora kaam dobara). Chhote transactions retries ko sasta banate hain. Deadline soft hai -- simple implementation, lekin overshoot possible.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Abort ke baad connection pool mein wapas nahi gaya -> pool leak. Statement retry -> inconsistent data. Commit timeout -> retry -> double effect.
advanced.alternatives: DB-side statement_timeout / idle_in_transaction timeout, saga pattern for cross-service work, outbox.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: High contention par serialization failures badhte hain -> retries badhte hain -> aur contention. Budget aur jitter yahan zaroori; ya design change (row-level partitioning).
advanced.production_improvements: Transaction ke liye alag policy naam aur onEvent metrics; deadlock/serialization retry count ka dashboard; idempotency key on writes.

question: You put a CircuitBreaker in front of a read replica. When it opens, should reads fall back to the primary? Design it.
answer_hinglish:
Pehle clear: is project mein DB nahi hai, aur library mein fallbacks implement nahi hain (README 'NOT implemented': 'Hedged requests, adaptive concurrency, fallbacks, caching'). Toh fallback app code mein likhna hoga: replica policy BrokenCircuitError throw kare toh catch karke primary par bhejo.

Lekin 'should' ka jawab: carefully, aur limited. Replica isliye hai ki primary ka read load kam ho. Agar replica down hua aur saare reads primary par chale gaye, toh primary par achanak 2x-10x load -- aur primary writes bhi sambhalta hai. Ab ek replica outage poore system ka outage ban sakta hai. Isliye:
1. Fallback ko apna alag bulkhead do ('primary-fallback', chhota maxConcurrent) -- taaki fallback primary ki capacity ka ek fixed hissa hi le sake. Baaki reads ko 503 milna better hai.
2. Sirf critical reads fallback karein (checkout), non-critical (recommendations) fail ya cached/stale data.
3. Replica lag bhi ek failure mode hai -- breaker sirf errors/timeouts dekhta hai, stale data nahi. Lag check alag.
4. Breaker isFailure: connection errors aur timeouts failure, query errors nahi.

Breaker ke defaults: windowSize 20, minimumCalls 10, failureRateThreshold 0.5, openMs 30 s, aur half-open mein 1 probe. Open ke dauraan replica ko zero load -- recovery ka time milta hai.
why_needed: Fallback bina capacity planning ke failure ko ek jagah se doosri jagah shift karta hai -- usually zyada important jagah par.
real_world_analogy: Highway band hua toh traffic ko village road par bhej diya -- ab village road bhi jam aur ambulance bhi phansi. Diversion par bhi limit chahiye.
how_it_works: Open state mein execute() operation call hi nahi karta: `throw new BrokenCircuitError('open', retryAfterMs)`. App ka catch error.state aur retryAfterMs dekh sakta hai. Half-open lazily next call par check hota hai, koi timer nahi.
in_this_project: src/breaker.ts state machine aur generations. Library mein fallback ka koi API nahi -- wrap() sirf policies compose karta hai. isRetryableHttp BrokenCircuitError ko non-retryable maanta hai, toh outer retry replica breaker ko hammer nahi karta.
advantages: Critical reads replica outage mein bhi chal sakti hain
Primary ke liye capped exposure
disadvantages: Fallback code app ka maintenance
Primary par extra load ka risk
Replica lag breaker se nahi pakda jaata
common_mistakes: Unbounded fallback to primary
Breaker ko lag detection samajhna
Fallback ko bhi wahi replica breaker se wrap karna
follow_up_questions: Multiple replicas ho toh per-replica breaker ya ek?
Stale cache fallback better hai ya primary?
Primary ka breaker bhi khul jaaye toh?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Fallback availability badhata hai lekin blast radius bhi badha sakta hai. Bounded fallback (alag bulkhead) beech ka raasta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Replica down -> saare reads primary -> primary slow -> writes fail -> full outage. Per-process breakers: har replica process alag time par khulta hai, toh fallback load gradually aata hai, ek saath nahi.
advanced.alternatives: Cache-aside stale reads, multiple replicas behind a load balancer, read-your-writes routing, degraded responses.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x reads par primary fallback bilkul impossible ho sakta hai -- tab degrade karo ya cache. Process-local breaker state har replica ko alag se seekhne deta hai (README: three replicas have three of each).
advanced.production_improvements: Fallback rate ka metric (breaker-rejected events + fallback counter), replica lag alerting, fallback bulkhead ka size primary capacity se derive.

question: Where should you create the policy objects in an Express or NestJS app, and what goes wrong if you create them inside the request handler?
answer_hinglish:
Module level par ya ek singleton service mein -- ek baar, per dependency. README ka pehla comment yahi hai: 'One set of policies PER DEPENDENCY, created once (module level / a singleton service), shared by every call.'

Kyun: CircuitBreaker ki state (closed/open, sliding window), RetryBudget ke tokens, aur Bulkhead ka `active` count -- yeh sab instance ke andar memory mein hain. Agar tum har request mein `new CircuitBreaker()` banaoge, toh har request ko ek fresh, closed breaker milega jisne kabhi failure dekha hi nahi -- breaker kabhi nahi khulega. Har request ka naya Bulkhead matlab har request ke paas apne 20 slots -- limit kuch limit nahi karti. Naya RetryBudget hamesha full -- retry storm protection gayab.

TimeoutPolicy aur RetryPolicy (bina budget) stateless jaise hain, toh unhe har baar banana galat nahi, bas bekaar allocation hai.

Express mein: ek `sms.ts` module jo `wrap(...)` export kare. NestJS mein: ek @Injectable service (default singleton scope) jo constructor mein policies banaye. Nest ke request-scoped providers mein policies mat rakhna -- woh har request ke liye naye bante hain. Nest test mein policies module-level variables hain ('Nest DI is not the point of these tests').
why_needed: Stateful policies ki value hi shared state hai. Per-request instance unhe silently bekaar bana deta hai -- koi error nahi, bas protection gayab.
real_world_analogy: Building ka fire alarm har visitor ke saath naya nahi lagta. Agar har aadmi apna naya alarm laaye jisne kabhi dhuan dekha hi nahi, toh aag lagne par koi alarm nahi bajega.
how_it_works: Policies plain classes hain; state instance fields mein (`current`, `ring`, `tokens`, `active`, `queue`). Koi global registry nahi -- sharing sirf same object reference se.
in_this_project: README `const sms = wrap(...)` module level par; express.test.ts mein policy `beforeEach` mein ek baar banti hai aur saari requests share karti hain; nestjs.test.ts mein breaker module-level `let breaker` hai.
advantages: Shared state se breaker/budget/bulkhead kaam karte hain
Kam allocations
disadvantages: Module-level state tests mein reset karna padta hai (beforeEach)
Per-process hi shared, cluster-wide nahi
common_mistakes: Handler ke andar policies banana
Nest request-scoped provider mein rakhna
Do alag dependencies ke liye ek hi breaker share karna

Do alag SMS providers -- kitne breakers?

question: How do you wire the Express adapter into an existing app, and why does the order of app.use matter?
answer_hinglish:
Teen cheezein, aur order important hai:
1. Route handler mein `requestSignal(req, res)` ko policy.execute ka doosra argument banao, aur try/catch karke `next(e)` -- kyunki Express 4 async handler ka rejected promise khud nahi pakadta (README example exactly yahi karta hai).
2. `loadShedding(bulkhead)` jis route ko protect karna ho uske pehle (`app.use('/heavy', ...)` ya route-level middleware).
3. `app.use(resilienceErrorHandler())` SAARE routes ke BAAD, aur tumhare apne final error handler se PEHLE.

Kyun order: Express middleware ko registration order mein chalata hai. Error middleware sirf unhi errors ko dekhta hai jo usse pehle registered routes ne next(e) se bheje. Routes se pehle register kiya toh woh kabhi chalega hi nahi. Aur agar tumhara generic 500 handler usse pehle laga, toh woh sab errors kha jaayega aur BrokenCircuitError ko bhi 500 bana dega -- 503 + Retry-After kabhi nahi jaayega.

question: How would you build dashboards and alerts for these policies using onEvent?
answer_hinglish:
Har policy `name` aur `onEvent` leti hai, aur ek hi handler ek typed union receive karta hai: `timeout`, `retry` (attempt, delayMs, error), `give-up` (attempts, reason, error), `breaker-state` (from, to), `breaker-rejected` (state), `bulkhead-rejected` (running, queued). Har event mein `policy` field hota hai (name, default kind). events.ts ka comment exact pattern deta hai: `onEvent: (e) => metrics.inc(\`resilience_${e.type}\`, { policy: e.policy })`.

Dashboard:
- Counter per type per policy: retries/sec, give-ups by reason (attempts, not-retryable, budget, deadline, retry-after-too-long), timeouts/sec, rejections.
- breaker-state transitions as annotations (closed->open ek incident marker hai).
- Gauges polling se: `bulkhead.running`, `bulkhead.queued`, `breaker.state`, `breaker.failureRate`, `budget.available` -- yeh getters hain, events nahi.

Alerts: breaker open > N minutes; give-up reason 'budget' ka spike (dependency down hai aur retries throttled); bulkhead-rejected rate (capacity kam); timeouts ka jump (latency regression).

Important safety: `emit()` handler ka throw nigal leta hai -- 'telemetry never changes what the caller gets' (tested; mutation E1). Lekin handler synchronous call hota hai, toh slow handler (sync network logging) har call slow karega. Cardinality: `error` object ko label mat banao -- sirf type/policy/reason.
why_needed: Resilience policies chupke se kaam karti hain -- agar metrics nahi, toh breaker hafton se khul-band ho raha hai aur kisi ko pata nahi.
real_world_analogy: Car ke dashboard par warning lights: engine theek chal raha hai kyunki ABS ne kaam kiya -- lekin light jalni chahiye taaki aap service karwao.
how_it_works: emit(handler, event): handler undefined -> return; warna try { handler(event) } catch {}. Policies emit karti hain: timeout timer par, retry sleep se pehle, give-up rethrow se pehle, breaker transition() mein, rejection par.
in_this_project: src/events.ts (ResilienceEvent union, emit). wrap.test.ts: 'timeout, retry, give-up, breaker-state, breaker-rejected, bulkhead-rejected -- with names', 'default policy names are their kinds', 'a throwing event handler changes nothing for the caller'. Purane callbacks (onRetry, onGiveUp, onStateChange) bhi chalte hain. Library khud koi metrics backend integrate nahi karti.

Throwing handler safe
Typed union -- switch exhaustive
disadvantages: Gauges ke liye polling khud karni padti hai
Sync handler -- slow handler hot path slow karta hai
Koi built-in metrics exporter nahi
common_mistakes: Error message ko metric label banana (cardinality explosion)

question: Why does requestSignal listen on the response's 'close' event and not the request's, and what happens end to end when a client disconnects?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki Node 16 se `req` ka 'close' event tab fire hota hai jab request body read ho jaati hai -- yeh disconnect nahi hai. Agar hum req 'close' par abort karte, toh POST /notify jaisi har request body parse hote hi abort ho jaati, aur SMS call kabhi poori nahi hoti. `res` ka 'close' connection band hone par fire hota hai, aur wahi sahi signal hai. Lekin res 'close' normal finish ke baad bhi aata hai, isliye check: `if (!res.writableFinished) controller.abort(new ClientClosedError())`. Matlab sirf tab abort jab response poora bheja nahi gaya.

End to end jab client chala jaata hai:
1. res 'close' -> signal aborted, reason ClientClosedError.
2. Yeh signal policy.execute ka caller signal hai. TimeoutPolicy use apne controller se link karta hai -> operation ka signal abort -> fetch upstream request cancel karta hai, upstream ko connection close dikhta hai.
3. RetryPolicy: 'failure after the caller aborted is never retried' -> caller ka reason throw. Backoff sleep bhi cancel.
4. Bulkhead queue mein tha toh queue chhod deta hai. Breaker aise call ko record nahi karta (dependency ki galti nahi).

Tests: express.test.ts 'the client disconnects -> the upstream request is cancelled (the upstream sees the close)', aur Nest mein bhi same. Mutations: A2 (request ka close) 2 tests, A1 (finished response ke baad bhi abort) 3 tests, A3 (per-response cache nahi) 1 test.
why_needed: Client chala gaya toh uske liye kaam karna -- retries, upstream calls, DB queries -- pure waste hai, aur overload mein yeh waste dusron ki capacity khaata hai.
real_world_analogy: Customer ne phone kaat diya; call center agent ko turant pata chalna chahiye taaki woh uske liye form bharna band kare -- yeh nahi ki 'customer ne baat karna band kiya' ko 'phone kat gaya' samajh le.
how_it_works: requestSignal: WeakMap<ServerResponse, AbortSignal> se per-response cache (dono adapters ya loadShedding + handler ek hi signal share karte hain). `res.once('close', ...)`. WeakMap isliye ki response garbage collect ho toh entry bhi chali jaaye.
in_this_project: src/adapters/express.ts requestSignal(); ClientClosedError src/errors.ts mein. http-status.test.ts unit tests fake EventEmitter response ke saath: same signal for same response; abort on early close; no abort after writableFinished. Nest ka @RequestSignal() isi function ko call karta hai.
advantages: Client chala gaya toh poori chain turant rukti hai
Ek signal per response -- loadShedding aur handler consistent
Framework-free (Node http types)
disadvantages: Abort ke baad bhi jo operation signal ignore kare woh chalta rahega
Proxies/load balancers ke peeche client disconnect hamesha propagate nahi hota
common_mistakes: req.on('close') use karna
writableFinished check bhoolna -- har finished response ke baad abort
Signal ko policy tak pass hi na karna
follow_up_questions: Load balancer client disconnect ko backend tak propagate karta hai?
Non-idempotent write ke beech client chala gaya toh cancel karna chahiye?

question: How does this library behave during a graceful shutdown (SIGTERM during a deploy), and what would you add?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha jawab: library mein graceful shutdown ka koi feature nahi hai -- na drain API, na 'stop accepting' mode, na shutdown signal. Toh behaviour poora app ke shutdown code par depend karta hai. Main batata hoon jo pieces hain, aur kya missing hai.

Jo exist karta hai: (1) `requestSignal` res 'close' par abort karta hai agar response finish nahi hua. Toh agar shutdown ke end mein app `server.closeAllConnections()` karta hai, toh in-flight requests ke signals ClientClosedError se abort honge -- retries rukengi, backoff sleeps cancel, upstream fetch cancel. (2) Bulkhead ke `running` aur `queued` getters -- shutdown code poll kar sakta hai ki in-flight calls zero hue ya nahi. (3) Breaker lazy hai, koi timer nahi; TimeoutPolicy aur sleep apne timers clear karte hain (tested: 'no timer left') -- toh library process ko zinda nahi rakhti.

Jo missing hai: `server.close()` sirf naye connections band karta hai; in-flight request ka signal abort nahi hota, toh woh poori retry chain (maxAttempts x timeout + waits) chala sakti hai, shutdown grace period se lamba. Ek shutdown-wide AbortController chahiye jo har requestSignal ke saath combine ho (AbortSignal.any, Node 20.3+ -- engines mein yahi minimum hai), aur loadShedding ko 'draining' mode jo naye requests ko 503 de.

Order: readiness fail -> drain wait (bulkhead.running == 0 ya timeout) -> abort shutdown signal -> closeAllConnections.
why_needed: Deploys roz hote hain. Agar shutdown in-flight calls ko beech mein kaat de toh har deploy par errors aur duplicate retries.
real_world_analogy: Dukaan band karne ka sahi tareeka: shutter aadha girao (naye customer nahi), andar walon ka bill banao, phir poora band. Library ke paas shutter nahi hai, sirf andar walon ki ginti hai.
how_it_works: Abort chain: res close -> requestSignal abort -> TimeoutPolicy ka onCallerAbort -> operation signal abort; RetryPolicy `signal?.aborted` -> throw reason; sleep(ms, signal) reject. Bulkhead waiter abort par queue se nikalta hai.
in_this_project: Repo mein koi shutdown code nahi -- tests `server.closeAllConnections()` aur `server.close()` afterEach mein use karte hain, bas. README 'NOT implemented' mein shutdown explicitly listed nahi hai, lekin code mein koi drain/shutdown API nahi hai. package.json engines: node >=20.3.

Koi background timers nahi jo process ko latkayein
running/queued se drain observe ho sakta hai
disadvantages: Drain/shutdown API nahi
server.close() akela in-flight retries nahi rokta
loadShedding mein draining mode nahi
common_mistakes: Sochna server.close() in-flight requests abort karta hai
Grace period retry chain ke worst case se chhota rakhna
Shutdown par abort karna non-idempotent writes ke beech mein bina soche

Worker (queue consumer) ka shutdown kaise alag hai?

advanced.failure_scenarios: SIGKILL grace period ke baad -> in-flight writes beech mein -> ambiguous state. Retry chain worst case (3 x 2 s + waits, deadline 8 s README example mein) grace se lamba.
advanced.alternatives: Framework-level shutdown hooks (Nest enableShutdownHooks), load balancer connection draining, AbortSignal.any se ek global shutdown signal.

question: How do you choose the numbers -- timeout, maxAttempts, deadlineMs, openMs, bulkhead size -- for a real dependency?
answer_hinglish:
Numbers dependency ke measured behaviour aur apne caller ke budget se aate hain, library defaults se nahi. Library defaults ek starting point hain: maxAttempts 3, backoff 100 ms x2 max 10 s full jitter, maxRetryAfterMs 60 s, breaker 0.5 / window 20 / minimumCalls 10 / openMs 30 s / 1 probe, RetryBudget 10 tokens / 0.1.

Mera process (generic guidance, is repo mein production data nahi hai):
1. Outer budget pehle: incoming request ka timeout (jaise client/LB 10 s). deadlineMs usse chhota, aur yaad rakho deadline soft hai -- last attempt ek timeout tak overshoot kar sakta hai. README example: per-attempt 2000 ms, 3 attempts, deadlineMs 8000.
2. Per-attempt timeout: dependency ke latency percentiles se -- typically p99 ke thoda upar, taaki normal slow calls kill na hon lekin hangs jaldi katein.
3. maxAttempts: 2-3; zyada sirf jab Retry-After/budget hai. Har attempt caller ka time khaata hai.
4. Bulkhead: Little's law (generic): concurrency ~ peak throughput x latency, thodi headroom; per process, toh replicas se divide. README example 20 + queue 50.
5. openMs: dependency ki typical recovery time; bahut chhota toh probes bar-bar fail, bahut bada toh recovery ke baad bhi users ko 503.
6. Breaker window/minimumCalls: low traffic par chhota window purane outcomes kam rakhta hai, lekin minimumCalls noise rokta hai.

Phir onEvent metrics se tune karo -- give-up reasons ka distribution batata hai kaunsa number galat hai.
why_needed: Galat numbers resilience ko hi failure source bana dete hain: chhota timeout healthy calls kaatta hai, bada timeout threads/sockets bhar deta hai, bahut retries storm laate hain.
real_world_analogy: Train ka time-table: aapki meeting 10 baje hai (outer deadline), toh aap 9:40 wali train ka wait 5 min karte ho (per-attempt timeout), nahi aayi toh agli -- lekin teesri train ka wait nahi karte kyunki meeting chhoot jaayegi (deadline).
how_it_works: Total worst case retry chain = maxAttempts x timeout + saare backoff waits (ya Retry-After), cap: deadlineMs + ek attempt ka timeout. Bulkhead slot sirf ek attempt tak hold hota hai (timeout andar, bulkhead retry ke andar).
in_this_project: README 'Use it' example ke numbers (sms: maxAttempts 3, deadlineMs 8000, bulkhead 20/50, timeout 2000) illustrative hain, measured nahi. Defaults retry.ts, backoff.ts, breaker.ts, budget.ts mein. Overhead bench (Windows, Ryzen 5 4500, Node 20.20.1) dikhata hai ki saari 4 policies saath ~11-12 microseconds per call (11356 / 12075 ns) -- network call ke saamne negligible, toh tuning latency budget ke liye hai, CPU ke liye nahi.

Har number ek option hai, code change nahi
Events se tuning feedback
disadvantages: Library adaptive tuning nahi karti (adaptive concurrency implement nahi)
Per-process numbers -- replica count badle toh bulkhead bhi badlo
common_mistakes: Inner timeout x attempts > outer timeout -- client pehle hi chala gaya
Har dependency par same numbers
Defaults ko production-tested maan lena

Bulkhead full ho rahi hai -- size badhaoge ya timeout ghataoge?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Tight timeouts tail latency kam karte hain lekin false failures badhate hain; zyada attempts success rate badhate hain lekin latency aur load bhi. Har number ek trade-off hai, isliye measure karke chuno.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Nested timeouts inverted (inner > outer) -> abandoned work. openMs bahut chhota -> half-open flapping. Bulkhead bahut chhota -> normal peak par 503.
advanced.alternatives: Adaptive concurrency limits (Netflix-style), latency-based hedging, SLO-driven timeouts -- sab is library mein implement nahi.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x traffic par bulkhead size aur replica count dono badlenge; breaker window jaldi bharega (count-based) -- matlab time ke hisaab se zyada sensitive.
advanced.production_improvements: Har dependency ka config file mein, dashboards per policy name, give-up reason ratios par alerts, load test se numbers validate.

question: Your API runs as 6 replicas behind a load balancer. How do per-process breakers, budgets and bulkheads behave, and would you build shared state?
answer_hinglish:
Is library ka saara state ek process ki memory mein hai -- README 'NOT implemented': 'Anything shared between processes... Three API replicas have three of each (each replica learns on its own that a dependency is down).' PLAN mein bhi 'Distributed state (a breaker shared between processes through Redis)' not in scope hai.

6 replicas mein:
- Breaker: har replica apne traffic se seekhta hai. Dependency down hui toh har replica ko minimumCalls (default 10) failures tak calls bhejne padte hain -- toh total ~6 x (kuch) calls failure detection mein. Recovery par har replica apna probe bhejta hai -- 6 probes, 1 nahi. Usually theek hai; bonus: ek replica ka network issue sirf usi ka breaker kholta hai (jo sahi bhi hai).
- Budget: per process, lekin ratio-based hai, toh har replica khud ~10% retry tak limit hota hai -- aggregate ratio bhi roughly wahi rehta hai. Fixed-count limit hoti toh replicas ke saath multiply hoti.
- Bulkhead: yeh sach mein multiply hota hai. maxConcurrent 20 x 6 = 120 concurrent calls dependency par. Agar dependency 50 sambhal sakti hai toh per-replica limit ~8 rakhni padegi, aur autoscaling par yeh number galat ho jaata hai.

Shared state banaoge? Mera recommendation: breaker aur budget ke liye nahi -- Redis ek naya failure point aur har call par latency laata hai, aur local learning kaafi fast hai. Bulkhead ke liye agar dependency ki hard limit hai toh ek distributed concurrency limit (ya provider-side rate limit) sochna padega -- lekin pehle replica-aware sizing se kaam chalao.
why_needed: Horizontally scaled services mein process-local limits multiply hote hain. Kaunsa state local chal sakta hai aur kaunsa nahi -- yeh classic distributed systems decision hai.
real_world_analogy: 6 shops ek hi godown se maal mangwaati hain. Har shop ka apna 'godown band hai' notice theek hai (har ek khud dekh leta hai), lekin agar har shop 20 trucks bheje toh godown ke gate par 120 trucks -- woh limit milke tay karni padegi.
how_it_works: Breaker: ring buffer aur generation counter instance par. Budget: integer tokens instance par. Bulkhead: `active` aur queue instance par. Koi persistence/sync nahi.

Har call par zero network overhead
Replica-specific failures sirf us replica ko affect karte hain
disadvantages: Bulkhead limits replicas ke saath multiply
Failure detection aur probes N guna
Autoscaling par sizing galat ho jaata hai
common_mistakes: Per-replica bulkhead ko global limit samajhna
Breaker ko Redis mein daal ke har call par network hop
Replicas badhaate waqt per-replica limits na ghataana
follow_up_questions: Distributed breaker banana ho toh Redis mein state kaise rakhoge?
Dependency hard rate limit deti hai (100 rps) -- 6 replicas mein kaise baantoge?

question: With loadShedding, what happens to a request whose client disconnects while it is running, or while it is waiting in the queue?
answer_hinglish:
Dono cases mein slot ya queue position free hoti hai -- yahi loadShedding ki correctness hai.

Running request: shedLoad() bulkhead.execute() ko ek operation deta hai jo ek promise return karta hai jo `res.once('close')` par resolve hota hai. Node mein res 'close' dono situations mein aata hai -- response finish hone ke baad bhi, aur connection beech mein toot jaane par bhi. Toh client chala gaya -> res close -> promise resolve -> bulkhead ka finally release() -> slot free (ya directly agle waiter ko hand off). Mutation A8 ('loadShedding frees the slot only on finish (not on a disconnect)') isi ko todta hai, aur test 'loadShedding: a client that disconnects mid-request frees its slot' use pakadta hai: running 1 hota hai, client abort, phir running 0.

Queued request (maxQueue > 0): bulkhead.execute ko `requestSignal(req, res)` diya jaata hai. Client gaya -> signal abort (ClientClosedError) -> Bulkhead ka waiter onAbort chalata hai -> queue se splice -> reject. loadShedding ka catch sirf BulkheadRejectedError par 503 likhta hai; ClientClosedError par kuch nahi bhejta -- comment: 'the client is gone, nothing to answer.'

Bina iske kya hota: har disconnect ek slot leak karta, aur thodi der mein saare slots 'zombie' requests ke paas -- har nayi request ko 503. Overload ke time disconnects sabse zyada hote hain, toh yeh bug exactly galat waqt par hit karta.
why_needed: Slot leak sabse khatarnaak failure hai kyunki woh dheere-dheere hota hai aur end mein poori service ko 503 de deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Parking mein gaadi bina ticket scan kiye nikal gayi -- agar counter ghatta nahi, toh kuch dino mein board 'FULL' dikhayega jabki parking khaali hai.
how_it_works: Bulkhead.execute: slot lo -> `try { return await operation(signal) } finally { this.release() }`. Operation ka promise res close par resolve. Waiter: signal par 'abort' listener jo queue se nikaal ke reject karta hai; hand-off par listener remove (mutation K7).
in_this_project: src/adapters/express.ts loadShedding(); src/bulkhead.ts waitForSlot()/release(). test/express.test.ts do loadShedding tests (Bulkhead maxConcurrent 2, maxQueue 0). Queue wala disconnect path (maxQueue > 0) Express test mein directly nahi hai; bulkhead.test.ts 'a queued caller that aborts leaves the queue, never runs, and its place is free' Bulkhead level par cover karta hai.

Queued disconnect queue chhod deta hai
Test se proven (A8)
disadvantages: Slot client ke jaane par free hota hai, lekin handler ka background kaam (agar signal use nahi kiya) chalta reh sakta hai
Queue-path ka Express-level test nahi

Queued request ke liye 503 likhne ki koshish jab client ja chuka

question: A TimeoutError reaches the error handler after the response has already started streaming. What do the Express and NestJS adapters do, and why?
answer_hinglish:
Dono adapters `res.headersSent` check karte hain, kyunki headers jaane ke baad status code badalna possible hi nahi -- 200 already wire par hai.

Express (resilienceErrorHandler): `if (mapped === undefined || res.headersSent) { next(error); return; }`. Yaani woh 504 likhne ki koshish nahi karta (karta toh ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT). Error ko aage bhej deta hai. Express ka default handler, headers bhej chuke response par, connection close kar deta hai (Express ka documented behaviour) -- client ko truncated response milta hai, jo sahi signal hai ki kuch galat hua. App ka apna error handler bhi isse pehle chal sakta hai -- use bhi headersSent check karna chahiye.

NestJS (ResilienceExceptionFilter): `if (res.headersSent) { res.destroy(); return; }` -- filter khud socket tod deta hai. Kyunki Nest filter ke paas next() nahi hai; yeh exception yahin handle hona hai. destroy() se client ko pata chalta hai ki response incomplete hai, bajaye ek 'complete' dikhne wale aadhe JSON ke.

Kab hota hai: streaming responses (res.write chunks, server-sent events) jahan handler pehle headers bhej deta hai phir dependency ko call karta hai. Normal `res.json(await ...)` pattern mein headers await ke baad jaate hain, toh yeh case nahi aata.

Honest note: is headersSent branch ka dedicated test express.test.ts ya nestjs.test.ts mein nahi dikha.
why_needed: Partial response ko 'success' jaisa dikhne dena data corruption ki tarah hai -- client aadha JSON parse karke galat conclusion nikaal sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Live TV par anchor ne news padhni shuru kar di, beech mein feed toot gayi. Aap 'yeh news galat hai' ka title wapas nahi badal sakte -- bas broadcast kaat sakte ho taaki koi aadhi news ko poori na samjhe.
how_it_works: HTTP mein status line aur headers pehle jaate hain. Ek baar res.writeHead/flush ho gaya, status fixed. Sirf do options: body continue karo ya connection abort karo (chunked encoding mein abort karne par client ko incomplete message error milta hai).
in_this_project: src/adapters/express.ts resilienceErrors(); src/adapters/nestjs.ts catch(). Nest filter `mapResilienceError(exception)!` non-null assertion use karta hai kyunki @Catch list wahi teen classes hain jo mapping karti hai.
advantages: Headers-sent case mein crash nahi (ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT avoid)

question: What breaks if the resilience error classes are loaded twice in the same process, and where did this project actually see it?
answer_hinglish:
Saari mapping `instanceof` par chalti hai. Agar errors.ts do baar load ho gaya (do module copies), toh BrokenCircuitError ki do alag classes exist karti hain. Breaker copy A ki class throw karta hai, adapter copy B ki class se check karta hai -> `instanceof` false. Nateeja:
1. mapResilienceError undefined return karta hai -> Express middleware next(error) -> app ka 500, 503 + Retry-After nahi.
2. Nest ka `@Catch(BrokenCircuitError, ...)` match nahi karta -> Nest ka default 500.
3. Sabse khatarnaak: isRetryableHttp `instanceof BrokenCircuitError` false paata hai, phir `!(error instanceof HttpError)` -> true. Matlab breaker rejection ko RETRYABLE maan liya -- jo K9 mutation ka exact bug hai: open breaker par retries.

Yeh project mein actually dikha -- test environment mein. README: stage 2 ke mutation runs ke counts unstable the, failures padhte the 'expected BulkheadRejectedError to be an instance of BulkheadRejectedError'. Cause: runner ne vitest ko lowercase drive path (`h:\...`) se start kiya, aur modules do baar load hue. Uppercase `H:\` se same breaks 3/3 runs mein same counts. Lesson README mein: noisy mutation count ek break ko caught dikha sakta hai jabki nahi hai -- unexpected failures ko naam se check karo.

Production analog: node_modules mein library ki do versions (nested install), ya bundler jo ek module do baar include kare. Library mein iska koi defense nahi hai (jaise `Symbol.for` brand ya `name` check) -- yeh limitation hai.
why_needed: instanceof-based dispatch silently fail hota hai -- koi exception nahi, bas galat branch. Aur yahan galat branch ka matlab retry storm ya galat status code hai.
real_world_analogy: Do printing press ne same design ka ID card chhapa. Guard sirf 'press A ka card' pehchanta hai -- press B ka bilkul same dikhne wala card reject. Asli employee bahar khada hai.
how_it_works: JS mein `x instanceof C` check karta hai ki C.prototype x ki prototype chain mein hai. Do module instances = do alag class objects = do alag prototypes. ESM module cache resolved URL/path se key hota hai; Windows par `h:` vs `H:` alag key ban sakte hain.
in_this_project: src/adapters/http-status.ts aur src/http.ts dono instanceof use karte hain; src/adapters/nestjs.ts @Catch class list. README 'A test-environment finding' section. Package `type: module` hai aur sirf ESM build (dist/) hai, CJS build nahi -- toh ESM/CJS dual-package hazard is package mein nahi hai, lekin duplicate install ka risk hai.

question: How does the NestJS adapter work -- @RequestSignal, the exception filter, why platform-express only, and why @nestjs/common is an optional peer dependency?
answer_hinglish:
Nest adapter do cheezein deta hai, dono Express adapter ke upar bane hain.

1. `@RequestSignal()` -- ek param decorator, `createParamDecorator` se. Woh `ctx.switchToHttp()` se request aur response leta hai aur seedha Express adapter ka `requestSignal(req, res)` call karta hai. Toh Nest controller ko bhi wahi per-response AbortSignal milta hai jo client disconnect par ClientClosedError se abort hota hai. Mutation A10 (signal jo kabhi abort nahi hota) Nest test se pakda gaya.

2. `ResilienceExceptionFilter` -- `@Catch(BrokenCircuitError, BulkheadRejectedError, TimeoutError)`. Sirf yeh teen classes; baaki exceptions Nest ki apni handling (test: `/boom` par `{statusCode: 500, message: 'Internal server error'}`). Same mapResilienceError -> 503/503/504. Register: `app.useGlobalFilters(new ResilienceExceptionFilter())`. Mutation A9 (filter response nahi likhta) 3 tests fail.

Platform-express only kyun: dono pieces response ko Node ka `ServerResponse` maan ke use karte hain -- `res.once('close')`, `res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader`, `res.end`. platform-express par Nest ka response Express ka res hai jo ServerResponse extend karta hai. Fastify par getResponse() FastifyReply deta hai -- alag API, toh yeh code wahan kaam nahi karega. README: 'NestJS only on platform-express (not Fastify)'.

Optional peer dependency: sirf `resilience-kit/nestjs` entry `@nestjs/common` import karti hai. Peer isliye ki user ki app ka hi Nest copy use ho (do copies = decorators/metadata ka mismatch). Optional isliye ki Express-only ya script users ko Nest install na karna pade.
why_needed: Framework adapter ko patla aur framework ke real objects ke saath tested hona chahiye; galat platform par silently galat behave karna worst case hai.
real_world_analogy: Universal charger ka adapter: plug wahi hai (core), sirf socket ke hisaab se chhota sa adapter. Lekin UK socket ka adapter US socket mein nahi lagta -- isliye packet par likha hai 'only for UK'.
how_it_works: createParamDecorator factory har request par chalti hai aur return value handler param ban jaati hai. @Catch(...) metadata se Nest exception ko class ke instanceof se filter se match karta hai. requestSignal WeakMap cache ki wajah se agar same response par do baar call ho toh same signal.

question: Design a Fastify (or Koa/Hono) adapter for this library. What must it provide, and what tests would prove it works?
answer_hinglish:
Pehle clear: README 'NOT implemented' mein hai -- 'no adapter for other frameworks (Koa, Hono)' aur NestJS Fastify par nahi. Toh yeh design hai, existing code nahi.

Adapter ko teen contracts poore karne hain, Express wale ki tarah:
1. Request signal: ek AbortSignal jo tab abort ho jab client response finish hone se pehle chala jaaye, reason ClientClosedError, ek per request (cache). Fastify mein raw Node objects `request.raw` aur `reply.raw` hain -- toh simplest design: `requestSignal(request.raw, reply.raw)` reuse karna, kyunki logic sirf ServerResponse ke 'close' aur writableFinished par hai. Koa mein `ctx.req`/`ctx.res` bhi raw Node objects hain. Hono (Web standard) mein Request ka apna `signal` hota hai, toh wahan alag mapping.
2. Error mapping: mapResilienceError() already framework-free hai (http-status.ts, core index se bhi export) -- adapter sirf framework ke error hook mein use call kare: Fastify `setErrorHandler`, Koa top middleware try/catch. Unknown errors ko framework ki default handling ko wapas dena -- Fastify mein `reply.send(error)` ya rethrow.
3. Load shedding: Fastify `onRequest` hook mein bulkhead slot lena aur `onResponse`/raw close par chhodna.

Tests (Express wale tests ka mirror, real app + real upstream): pass-through aur signal not aborted afterwards; hang -> 504; breaker -> 503 + Retry-After, upstream hits na badhein; unmapped error framework handler tak; upstream 401 -> 500; client disconnect -> upstream sees close; load shedding 3rd request 503 aur disconnect par slot free. Phir mutations A1-A11 jaise breaks.

question: Why are the adapters separate entry points (resilience-kit/express, resilience-kit/nestjs) instead of part of the core, and why is the 503/504 mapping in its own file?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki core ka promise hai 'framework-free, zero runtime dependency' -- same code Express handler, NestJS service, worker ya script mein chale. Agar adapters core index mein hote, toh `import { RetryPolicy } from 'resilience-kit'` bhi `@nestjs/common` load karne ki koshish karta -- ek worker jo Nest use hi nahi karta, crash karta ya Nest install karta. PLAN.md ka decision: 'Recommended over one package that imports both frameworks, which would force them on every user.'

Implementation: package.json `exports` map mein teen entries -- '.' -> dist/index.js, './express' -> dist/adapters/express.js, './nestjs' -> dist/adapters/nestjs.js. src/index.ts comment: 'Framework adapters are separate entry points ... so the core never pulls them in.' Express adapter toh Express import hi nahi karta -- sirf `import type` Node http se, jo compile ke baad gayab ho jaata hai. Nest adapter `@nestjs/common` import karta hai, isliye woh optional peer dependency hai.

http-status.ts alag kyun: 503/504 mapping ek policy decision hai jo dono adapters mein exactly same honi chahiye. Ek file = ek source of truth; Nest filter aur Express middleware dono `mapResilienceError()` call karte hain, sirf response likhne ka tareeka alag. Yeh framework-free bhi hai, isliye core index bhi ise export karta hai -- koi bhi naya adapter (ya app ka apna) ise reuse kar sakta hai. Tests bhi split: http-status.test.ts mapping ko unit level par, express/nestjs tests real apps par.
why_needed: Library design mein dependency direction sabse important hai: core kisi framework ko nahi jaanta, adapters core ko jaante hain. Ulta hua toh har user har framework ka bojh uthata hai.
real_world_analogy: Mobile phone mein USB-C port hai (core); car charger aur wall charger alag bikte hain (adapters). Phone ke andar car charger fit nahi kiya jaata.
how_it_works: Node ka package `exports` field subpath imports allow karta hai aur unlisted internal paths ko block karta hai. TypeScript `import type` runtime par emit nahi hota, isliye express.ts compiled JS mein express ka koi require/import nahi.
